heading: Lifecycle and events: Tac
summary: The same two roles in the browser and on native hosts, used by one component view. A browser resource is autowired by the field's name, which is the name Spring uses: view, lifecycle, resourceLoader, taskScheduler and applicationEventPublisher. An uninitialised applicationEventPublisher field is already that resource, so its annotation is optional. Native services have no browser resources. The prelude constructs a member of type ApplicationEventPublisher. An F# service takes its ApplicationEventPublisher as a primary constructor parameter, and Tachyon passes one when it creates the service. A Needs property, `[<Needs>] member val Publisher : ApplicationEventPublisher = Unchecked.defaultof<ApplicationEventPublisher> with get, set`, receives it the same way. A listener takes one model parameter, and the type of that model is the event that it hears. Write one method for each model; there is no list of events. The listener has the same condition, id, replay and Order options as in Yon. When a listener returns a model, Tachyon publishes the returned model as a new event, as settle does with SettledOrder; a returned `{event, value}` record is not read (ADR 0055). InBackground is allowed in every Tac language, because it delays delivery and does not need an asynchronous method. Native hooks and listeners stay synchronous. JavaScript and TypeScript bundle for the web. Swift builds for macOS, Kotlin for Android, C# for Windows and Rust for desktop Linux. A Rust or C# service with no browser script reaches the web, and every native target that does not link it, as WebAssembly, and a Go, Java or F# service always runs that way. A Java service declares an uninitialised ApplicationEventPublisher field (Needs is optional), and its listeners take one model from client/models. On the web, WebAssembly listeners share the page event bus with browser services, including conditions, Order, InBackground microtasks, retained replay and cleanup. Publications from any service reach its own listeners and other services exactly once. A Dart service is a browser service compiled to WebAssembly (WasmGC). Its only resource is the ApplicationEventPublisher that it declares with Needs. This publisher publishes through the page runtime, so Dart and JavaScript listeners receive the same events. Its lifecycle and listener methods are public and take JSON values, because the runtime calls them by name across the bridge. A Lua service (ADR 0085) writes each hook as a comment marker, such as `-- @OnStart` or `-- @OnEvent`, above its method. Its field `application_event_publisher = nil` is that resource, autowired by its name, and an event is a model table such as `setmetatable({ total = 25 }, PlacedOrder)`. A Python service (ADR 0093) writes `@on_start` above a plain or `async def` method and `@on_stop` and `@on_event` above plain methods, and an `application_event_publisher: ApplicationEventPublisher` field is that resource. Its events are dataclass models from client/models. A C++ service (ADR 0099) writes `[[OnStart]]`, `[[OnStop]]`, `[[OnEvent]]`, `[[Order(n)]]` and `[[InBackground]]` before its methods, and its `ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;` field is that resource. Its hooks and listeners may be private; its events are structs from client/models.
